storm.summary_layperson: Strong thunderstorm cells 17–25 miles away are closing in and expected to arrive between 6:45 and 7:45 PM; the Long Island Sound slows them slightly but will not stop the most intense cores tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water at 74°F versus 79°F air creates a weak stable layer — enough to potentially blunt the weakest lead cell, but the 62 dBZ cores behind it carry too much energy (2,070 J/kg) to be reliably stopped.
storm.detail_html:
A cluster of thunderstorm cells is currently 17 to 25 miles west-northwest of the cove, tracking northeast at 21 knots. The lead cell (35 dBZ at 17 miles) is relatively weak, but a tight group of 61–62 dBZ cores follows at 22–25 miles — well above the severe-weather threshold. An isolated severe thunderstorm is possible, though the NWS Area Forecast Discussion notes poor lapse rates and rates organized severe weather as unlikely for this specific area.

Based on radar-tracked storm motion, the expected arrival window for the cove is 6:46–7:46 PM, with a central estimate around 7:11 PM. Expect the outflow gust front to arrive 10–15 minutes ahead of visible rain. This timing falls squarely inside the evening race window. Confidence is medium — the motion is radar-measured rather than modeled, but the system is 60–90 minutes out and individual cells may regenerate or fade between now and arrival.

Long Island Sound provides a weak moderating influence tonight. With water at 74°F against 79°F air, the 5°F difference creates a thin stable boundary layer over the Sound. The storm approach angle from the WNW is nearly perpendicular to the Sound — the most favorable geometry for the water to weaken incoming cells — and the relatively slow 21-knot storm motion gives the Sound more time to act. These factors earn the cove a moderate Sound-effect rating: the weaker lead cell may shed its lightning or split at the coastline, but the 62 dBZ cores carry enough energy to push through. Expect somewhat less rain and thunder here than in towns 3–5 miles inland, though the margin is modest tonight.

The main limit on the Sound's protection is instability. At 2,070 J/kg, available convective energy exceeds the 1,500 J/kg level where the marine layer reliably chokes incoming storms. Combined with 13–15 knots of shear, these cells are organized enough to sustain themselves through the coastal boundary. Expect heavy rain, lightning, and wind gusts — likely 20–30 knots during the squall — for 20–40 minutes around arrival time.

What would change this picture: if the 62 dBZ cores weaken below 45 dBZ on live radar as they approach the CT coast (check KOKX by 6:15–6:30 PM), the Sound effect is working and risk drops to moderate. Conversely, if APRS stations to the west — GW2598 in Rye (9 miles WNW) or GW4034 in Port Chester (5 miles WSW) — spike above 20 knots gust before 6:30 PM, the outflow gust front is outrunning the cells and arrival will beat the predicted window by 10–15 minutes. A Flood Watch remains in effect through Tuesday morning, reflecting a broader wet pattern well beyond tonight's storm.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked lead cell 17 mi WNW closing at 9 kt, with intense 61–62 dBZ cores trailing at 22–25 mi; southerly onshore flow may retard the gust front slightly, but the main line should arrive within the window.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play

wind.tactics_blurb: S-to-SSW gradient wind enters the cove cleanly through its south-facing mouth, with fairly even pressure from shore to shore and a slight edge toward center and west. Start mid-line if racing before 6:30 PM — after that, the approaching storm makes this a safety call more than a tactics call.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight's wind is a moderate gradient southerly — no sea breeze is driving it. The air-to-water temperature difference of 4.5°F falls just below the 5°F gate needed for a thermally driven sea breeze, so the southerly flow is synoptic. The NWS forecast confirms south wind around 8 mph, and airport anemometers at Bridgeport, Islip, and Block Island average 7–11 knots — consistent with a light-to-moderate synoptic gradient.

Direction is the main complication for this forecast. The HRRR model shows SE (144°) for 17:00, but every local station — the cove's own weatherstation at SSW (205°), the buoy at S (190°), and APRS stations from Rye to Huntington — is already in southerly flow. The 60° model-to-observation gap matters: SE flow puts the cove in the partial shadow of Greenwich Point, while SSW flow enters cleanly up the cove axis. The 17:00 row uses the observed SSW direction; HRRR transitions to S by 19:00, which aligns better and is used for later hours. Lean toward what you see on the water rather than the raw model this evening.

In S-to-SSW flow, the cove's south-facing mouth receives wind cleanly. Pressure is fairly uniform across the course, with a slight channeling effect along the west shore (Belle Haven / Field Point side) in pure SSW — giving a marginal center-to-west edge, but not enough to commit hard to either side. The 10-minute average at the cove is currently 3.6 knots — noticeably lighter than the over-water buoy at 11 knots — reflecting some shelter in the current SE-influenced regional flow. As the direction consolidates toward S, in-cove speeds should build to 7–9 knots ahead of the storm.

The approaching storm dominates any tactical planning for the 19:00–21:00 window. The expected arrival between 6:46 and 7:46 PM brings a sudden outflow gust shift — wind will jump 15–25 knots and veer sharply before the rain arrives. Post-storm, the gradient collapses quickly; HRRR shows only 3–4 knots by 22:00. On a purely gradient day, evening wind would hold steadier — but with the storm acting as a circuit-breaker, any residual flow after passage will be weak and variable.

The best racing window is 17:00–18:30: 5–8 knots of mostly clean southerly flow, with manageable puffs and no storm risk yet. After 18:30, the arrival window opens and race committee should have a clear weather contingency before the start gun. If the storm tracks early and clears by 20:00, a brief 5–7 knot post-storm window may follow — but with HRRR showing only 3 knots by 22:00 and the gradient fading, count on one competitive race tonight rather than a full series.
